newsitem.title: DUBAI: Brother of victim in Saudi murder can demand death.
newsitem.headline: Brother of victim in Saudi murder can demand death.

text.p: The brother of an Australian nurse murdered in Saudi Arabia has been granted the right to demand execution if her alleged killers are found guilty, sources close to the case said on Tuesday.

An Islamic sharia court in the eastern Saudi city of Khobar, which has been hearing the controversial case since May, ruled that Frank Gilford could make the life-or-death decision as the closest relative of victim Yvonne Gilford, the sources said.

The ruling makes him a key player in the trial of Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, the two British nurses charged with killing their colleague in December at a medical complex in Dhahran, near Khobar.

"Frank is the one that when it comes down to it will have the right to make the decision about an execution," a source close to the proceedings told Reuters. Frank lives in Australia and has not attended the trial.
The breakthough decision ended weeks of deadlock over whether Gilford had the right to speak on behalf of the victim's closest family -- made up of their mother and himself.

Muriel Gilford, the 84-year-old mother of victim Yvonne Gilford, suffers from Alzheimer's disease and lives in a nursing home in Australia. The court had initially questioned whether the power of attorney Muriel had granted to her son was valid and had demanded additional documents.
"The judges now have all the necessary documentation," the source said. "The procedural issues are over. Now the judges will go over the case."

The court adjourned for an unspecified period on Monday for deliberation after the lawyers of the victim's family insisted on the death sentence, the defence lawyers from the Law Firm of Salah al-Hejailan said.
The court had urged the two parties to seek reconciliation even before a verdict is reached.
Jim Phipps, a lawyer at the International Law Firm which represents the Gilfords, said his firm had no comment.

According to Islamic sharia law practised in the conservative kingdom, the victim's heirs may decide for or against capital punishment if the court finds the accused guilty and says capital punishment is the justified sentence.
If Parry and McLauchlan are found guilty as charged, they could face public beheading by the sword, the common form of execution in Saudi Arabia.

The women have said they were forced into making confessions to the crime, which they later revoked. Both women, who are jailed in nearby Dammam but have attended every court session, say they are innocent.
Gilford was found stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated in her room at the King Fahd military medical complex just days before her 56th birthday.
The case has stirred up controversy since the women were arrested in December, sparking calls for a more open trial.
Saudi officials, who have barred journalists from the hearings, have repeatedly said the proceedings were fair and that the women had nothing to fear if they were innocent.
